en: The *Benevolent Vow Sutra of Bhaiṣajyaguru*, a commentary on the ancient traces [of this scripture],
compiled by the Śramaṇa Tae-hyeon of Cheonggyu. This sutra is briefly summarized in three [sections].
Analysis by Way of Chapters:
First, the title; second, the inclusion within the teaching; third, the main text.
Regarding the first, the title, the sutra has three names:
First, the *Sūtra on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha*;
second, the *Consecrated Mantra for the Twelve Divine Generals Who Benefit Sentient Beings*;
and third, the *Rite for Eradicating All Karmic Obstructions*.

Among these, the version translated during the first year of the Daming era in the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty adopted the third title, *The Sutra on the Eradication of Transgressions and Sins and Attaining Deliverance from Birth and Death*.

The version translated at the Translation Hall in the Upper Garden (Shanglin Yuan) south of Luoshui in the Eastern Capital in the eleventh year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty abbreviated the original title to *The Sutra of the Original Vows of the Medicine Master Tathāgata*.
The present version, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang during the Zhenguan era of the Great Tang, adopts the full original title as the title for this entire work.
The extensive and concise versions of the text are similar in their latter two sections.
"Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha Tathāgata" refers to the person to whom one should turn for refuge.
"The merit of his original vows" refers to the virtue that has been evoked.

One who can uproot all sufferings is metaphorically named "Medicine Master" (Bhaiṣajyaguru); one whose unconditioned compassion is all-pervasive is called "Lapis Lazuli Light" (Vaiḍūryaprabha). The sublime practices cultivated are termed "Original Vows," and the supreme fruit realized is termed "Merit.
Thus, the Tathāgata’s cause and effect constitute the central doctrine, while exhorting beings to take refuge and escape suffering constitutes the ultimate goal.
Therefore, the first title is designated by its primary essence (*mūla*), while the names of the latter two are designated by their purpose (*prayojana*).
"Sūtra" refers to the *sūtra* as a scripture; it is the name that expresses the meaning.
Because it accords with the meaning and binds together the vessels of the Dharma so they are not lost or dispersed, it is called a *sūtra*.

Because it concerns the merit of the original vows of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata and the sūtra of those original vows and merits, it is an *upapada-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound) according to the sixfold analysis of compounds (*ṣatprakāra-vigraha*).
Regarding its inclusion within the categories of teaching, the masters of the Southern Land say:
"The Buddha's teachings are threefold: first, the sudden; second, the gradual; and third, the partial and indeterminate teaching."

The first two [teachings] are as usual; however, the current *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* is subsumed under the third teaching, as it is taught restrictively according to specific conditions and differs from the sudden and gradual teachings.

This is not reasonable, because there is no awakening distinct from the sudden and gradual, nor can there be a separate teaching apart from the Great and Small Vehicles. Since it directly explains the causes, effects, and virtues of the Mahāyāna to Mañjuśrī, what is taught here is the Sudden Teaching.
Furthermore, because it explains that the Pure Land is characterized by the absence of obscuration, it is subsumed under the third category of the definitive Mahāyāna teachings.
Regarding the threefold textual form, this is a sūtra:
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Bhagavān was traveling through various countries for the sake of conversion when he arrived at the city of Vaiśālī and stayed beneath a tree named *Ratana-ghoṣa*. He was accompanied by a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus, thirty-six thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as kings, ministers, brahmins, lay devotees, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and other immeasurable multitudes who surrounded him with reverent devotion as he preached the Dharma.
The commentary states:

This text consists of three parts: first, the section on the occasion for the preaching of the sūtra; second, the section on the detailed exposition in response to questions; and third, the section on the joyful practice upon hearing the name.
This is the first.
"Thus have I heard," and so forth, should be understood as usual.
The term *Bhagavān* contains six meanings:
first, the meaning of sovereignty, because he is forever unbound by any afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second is the meaning of blazing intensity, because it is refined and tempered by the fierce flames of the fire of wisdom;
third is the meaning of sublime adornment, because it is adorned with the various wondrous marks and signs;
fourth is the meaning of renown, because its perfections of merit are such that there is nothing unknown.
Fifth is the sense of auspiciousness, because approaching and making offerings to it necessarily yields benefit;
sixth is the sense of nobility, because it possesses all virtues and brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings without indolence.

As stated in a verse of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*: "Sovereignty, brilliance, and physical excellence, renown, auspiciousness, and nobility—these six distinct meanings should be known as collectively termed 'Bhagavat'."
Regarding the term "Vaiśālī" (Broad and Pure), in Sanskrit it is called Vaiśālī or Vaidiśā; it signifies the fulfillment of manifold virtues.
Upon arriving at the city of Vaiśālī, he manifested the joy of sentient beings.

When the *nādī-vṛkṣa* (Sound-of-Music Trees) are inhabited and stirred by a gentle breeze, elegant sounds corresponding to the musical scales of *gong* and *shang* emerge from them; therefore, they are called Sound-of-Music Trees.
There are three kinds of assemblies:
first, the assembly of *śrāvakas*; second, the assembly of *bodhisattvas*; and third, the worldly assembly, which may be understood according to the text.
Among these, a *gṛhapati* (householder) is one who dwells at home.
A *yakṣa* means one who is formidable or possesses awesome power.

At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed toward the Bhagavat, joined his palms, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We only pray that you will proclaim the names of such Buddhas of similar character, as well as their original great vows and sublime merits, so that all who hear them may have their karmic obstructions eliminated, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings during the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails.”
The commentary states:
From here below begins the section on the detailed exposition in response to questions.
This consists of five points:

1. The accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s inquiry; 2. The accomplishment of the Dharma King’s approval; 3. The accomplishment of the assembly’s delight in hearing; 4. The accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma; 5. The accomplishment of the yakṣa’s requital of gratitude.
This is the first [section].
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the section on the causes and conditions for the request, as in the sutra: "The Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power... and so forth.

Mañjuśrī—translated into Chinese as Miaojixiang (Wondrous Auspiciousness)—is born through transformation from the Dharma and has attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma; thus he is called a Prince of the Dharma (*dharmarāja-putra*).
Regarding the second section, the Gate of Majestic Demeanor for the Request, it is as stated in the sutra: "Rising from his seat... up to joining his palms."
Rising from one’s seat signifies arising from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Baring one shoulder signifies performing deeds for the benefit and happiness of others.
Placing the right knee on the ground signifies abiding within the world.
"Facing the Bhagavān" means tending toward the supramundane.
"Bowing the body" means being free from pride.
"Joining the palms" means focusing the mind with single-minded devotion.
Third is the section on the formal invitation, as stated in the sutra: "He addressed the World-Honored One... for the sake of all sentient beings.
This briefly asks about three matters:
first, the inquiry regarding the Buddha’s name; second, the inquiry regarding his great vows as the cause; and third, the inquiry regarding his meritorious qualities as the fruit.
The passage beginning with "causing all who hear it" and following enumerates the benefits of its exposition.
Regarding the phrase "when the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka) turns," the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:

"There are six kinds of firmness: first, the firmness of the Dharma-body abiding; second, the firmness of liberation abiding; third, the firmness of meditative concentration abiding; fourth, the firmness of extensive learning abiding; fifth, the firmness of merit and virtue abiding; and sixth, the firmness of strife abiding."
Among these, the first period occurs while the Buddha is still in the world, and the subsequent five periods occur after his parinirvāṇa; each lasts for five hundred years respectively.
Taken collectively, they are called the three periods:
the first is the *saddharma* (True Dharma), which refers to the first two of those five periods during which the teachings remain firm and stable.
The second is the Semblance Dharma, which corresponds to the next two firmnesses;
the third is the Final Dharma, which corresponds to the last firmness.
These possess, respectively, the three aspects of teaching, practice, and fruition.
There are two [types of] non-resultant [actions];
there is informative action, but not the other two.
Now, for the sake of the benefit and happiness of sentient beings during the Semblance Dharma period a thousand years hence, I have posed this question.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Mañjuśrī!"

Out of great compassion, you have exhorted me to speak the names of the Buddhas and the merits of their original vows, for the sake of uprooting the sentient beings entangled by karmic obstructions, and to benefit, aid, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings during the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails.
"Listen now with close attention and reflect well; I shall speak for you.
Mañjuśrī replied, "Indeed, we pray that you will speak; we long to hear it."
The commentary states:
Herein there are two parts.
First is the accomplishment authorized by the Dharma King, as the sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One... shall explain it for you."
That which is heard should be remembered; because the initial words are excellent, one says "Excellent!
Because they are appropriate for the occasion, one again says "Excellent!
To cause the text to be examined with care, one says "Listen attentively!"
It is called "well-considered" because it causes the meaning to be understood.
Second, it is the accomplishment of the great assembly’s delight in hearing, as the sutra states: "Mañjuśrī said, 'Indeed, we wish to hear; please speak.'"
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:

"To the east of here, passing beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Vaidūryanirmala (Pure Lapis Lazuli). There, the Buddha is named Bhaisajyaguruvaidūryaprabhāsa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Hero, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The commentary states:
The fourth is the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of teaching the Dharma.
This consists of two gates:
First, the section on providing the correct answer to the request; second, the section on exhorting beings toward their benefit.
The first [section] also has three parts, as it answers three questions.
This is the first [of those].
The detailed explanation of the ten titles is as found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts. Mañjuśrī!
When that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he made twelve great vows so that all sentient beings might obtain whatever they seek.
The commentary states:
The response to the second question consists of three parts:
a brief indication, a detailed exposition, and a concluding summary.
This is the first [point].

The *Asura Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva Vairocanaprabha encountered the Buddha Jñānavijaya and first made his general vows; at the place of the Buddha Ratnaśikhin, he first made his specific vows."
The *Sūtra on the Manifestation of All Buddhas of the Ten Directions* states: "The twelve vows made by the Buddha Blue Dragon Light (*Nīlagarbhaprabha*).
The first great vow:

'May it be that when I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in a future age, my own radiance shall blaze forth, illuminating immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless worlds; may my body be adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary signs, and may all sentient beings become no different from me.'"
The second great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, my body shall be like lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out, pure and free from blemish, with vast radiance and towering merit. My body shall dwell in perfect stability, adorned by a web of flames surpassing the sun and moon. May all sentient beings in the dark realms receive illumination and clarity, performing all their various activities according to their inclinations.
The third great vow:

"May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, through immeasurable and boundless wisdom and skillful means, I shall cause all sentient beings to obtain inexhaustible objects of enjoyment, so that no being shall ever lack anything."
The fourth great vow:
"May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who practice deviant paths, I shall cause them all to dwell securely within the path of Bodhi;
and if there are those who practice the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, I shall establish them all in the Mahāyāna."
The fifth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are immeasurable and boundless sentient beings who practice the holy life within my Dharma, may I cause them all to obtain unimpaired precepts and be endowed with the three clusters of pure precepts;
should they happen to violate them, upon hearing my name, may they again attain purity and not fall into the evil realms.
The sixth great vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings whose bodies are inferior, whose faculties are incomplete, who are ugly, dull, or foolish, or who suffer from various ailments such as blindness, deafness, muteness, lameness, paralysis, hunchback, leprosy, or insanity—once they have heard my name, may they all become upright and wise, with all their faculties complete and free from all sickness and suffering.
The Seventh Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are oppressed by various illnesses, having no rescue, no refuge, no physician, no medicine, no kinsmen, and no home, and who suffer greatly from poverty—if my name should once reach their ears, may all their illnesses be completely eliminated, their bodies and minds become peaceful and happy, their families and provisions become fully abundant, and they shall even go on to realize unsurpassed Bodhi.
The Eighth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are women who are oppressed by the hundred evils of womanhood and, giving rise to extreme revulsion, wish to cast off their female bodies;
upon hearing my name, may they all transform from female to male, possess the marks of a man, and even go on to realize unexcelled Bodhi.
The ninth great vow:
May it be that when I attain enlightenment in a future life, I shall cause all sentient beings to emerge from the net of Māra and be liberated from the entanglements of all non-Buddhist paths;

if they have fallen into the dense forest of various evil views, I shall draw them in and establish them in right view, gradually leading them to practice the deeds of a bodhisattva and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Tenth Great Vow:

May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are punished by the laws of kings—being bound, beaten, imprisoned, or facing execution—and who suffer physical and mental agony due to being oppressed by countless other calamities and insults;
if they hear my name, by the power of my merit and majestic spiritual strength, may they all be liberated from all their sorrows and sufferings.
The eleventh great vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are tormented by hunger and thirst and commit various evil deeds for the sake of seeking food;

if they hear my name and single-mindedly remember and uphold it, I shall first satisfy their bodies with the most excellent and sublime food and drink, and subsequently establish them in ultimate peace and happiness through the flavor of the Dharma.
The Twelfth Great Vow:
May it be that when I attain Bodhi in a future life, if there are sentient beings who are poor and lack clothing, and are tormented day and night by mosquitoes, gadflies, cold, and heat;

if they hear my name and single-mindedly keep it in mind and uphold it, may they immediately obtain all kinds of superior and exquisite garments according to their preferences, and likewise obtain all manner of precious ornaments, flower garlands, scented ointments, drums, music, and various performances—fulfilling everything they enjoy according to their hearts' desire.
The commentary states:
Within the section on the extensive explanation of the gates, there are six pairs of gates.

First is the gate of benefiting the pure and the defiled, which refers to the first two vows; for [in these vows], all things in the Pure Land are like one's own body, and even sentient beings in the darkness between worlds follow their intentions.

The two gates of the mundane and supramundane realms correspond to the next two vows: because there is no lack in the vehicles of humans and devas, and because even those who practice wrong paths are established in the bodhi-path of the three vehicles according to their respective dispositions, while those of indeterminate lineage in the two vehicles are all established in the Mahāyāna.

The third is the gate of preserving the precepts and preserving the body, which refers to the following two vows: not violating the weighty precepts because one is endowed with the three clusters of pure conduct (*tri-skandha*), and because the body of the six sense faculties attains complete purity.
In this context, "inferior" does not include the introductory phrase.
Although they possess the various faculties, they are not superior or excellent because they are deficient.
The term "ugly" explains the inferiority of the body.
The term "obstinate and ignorant" explains the inferiority of the mental faculty (*manas*).
"Blind, deaf," and so forth, explain the non-possession of the faculties of eye, ear, tongue, and body.
"Insane" explains the non-possession of the mental faculty.
The various sufferings of illness include those of the nose and other sense organs.
The four qualities beginning with "handsome" are the opposites of the aforementioned [defects], respectively.
The four gates for eliminating internal and external suffering correspond to the following two vows: the first is able to eliminate the suffering of oppression from external conditions.
"Without rescue" indicates the absence of medicine;
"without refuge" indicates the absence of kin and so forth.
Now, having obtained the Buddha as physician, the Dharma as medicine, and the noble wealth, one is thus freed from illness and the like, even unto abundance.
Second, it can transform the internal condition of the female body and its suffering, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "All women are abodes where all manner of evils reside."

The fifth is the gate of liberation from internal and external fetters; this corresponds to the next two vows, which involve establishing oneself in right view to untie the bonds of false views, thereby realizing the unsurpassed path and escaping the snares of Māra.
By means of his majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*), he releases them from execution and bondage.

Regarding the sixth, the gate of food and clothing: this refers to the next two vows, because they establish [beings] with the flavor of the Dharma as their food and satisfy them with exquisite garments and the like.
Mañjuśrī! These are the twelve subtle and supreme vows that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, made while practicing the bodhisattva path.
The commentary states:
This is a summary. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

The great vows that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, made while practicing the bodhisattva path, as well as the meritorious adornments of that buddha-field, could not be fully described by me even in one kalpa, or more than one kalpa.

However, that buddha-field is exclusively pure; it has no women, nor are there any evil realms or sounds of suffering. Its ground is made of lapis lazuli, with roads demarcated by golden cords; its cities, palaces, towers, pavilions, balconies, windows, and lattices are all composed of the seven treasures. It is equal in its meritorious adornments to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, without any distinction.

In that land there were two bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, one named Sūryavairocana (Sunlight Pervading All) and the other named Candravairocana (Moonlight Pervading All). They were the leaders of those immeasurable and incalculable hosts of bodhisattvas, and they were all able to uphold the precious treasury of the True Dharma of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! All sons and daughters of good family who possess faith should aspire to be born in that Buddha-world.
Commentary:
This answers the subsequent question.
It contains two parts:
first, the accomplishment of the merit of adornment in its original location; second, the accomplishment of the merit of hearing the name in other regions.
This is the first point.
Regarding the statement that the adornments of the Buddha-land resulting from the great vows cannot be fully described, this reveals that the fruits of such great vows are likewise boundless;
the physical realm should correspond to these vows.
Briefly stated, that land is endowed with eight kinds of meritorious accomplishments:
first, the accomplishment of being free from all attachment and defilement, as the sutra says, "there are no women."
Second is the accomplishment of being free from the terrors of evil, as the sūtra states: "Furthermore, there are no evil destinies nor sounds of suffering.
Third is the accomplishment of the purity of the basis, as the sūtra states: "The ground is made of lapis lazuli."
Fourth is the accomplishment of the formation of the roads, as the sutra says, "the roads are demarcated by golden cords.
Fifth is the accomplishment of the adornment of the palaces, as the sutra says, "just like the western [pure land]."
The sixth is the accomplishment of the uninterrupted succession of the six great sages, as the sutra states: "There are two bodhisattvas," for they are those who occupy the position of the successor.
The seventh is the accomplishment of the uninterrupted continuity of benefit and happiness, as the sutra states: "They all uphold the treasury of the True Dharma of that Buddha."
Eighth is the accomplishment of birth without obstruction, as the sutra states: "One should aspire to be born in that Buddha-world.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying: "Mañjuśrī!"

There are sentient beings who do not distinguish between good and evil, harboring only greed and stinginess; they do not understand giving or the karmic fruits of giving. Foolish and lacking wisdom, they are deficient in the faculty of faith; they amass great wealth and labor to guard it, feeling no joy when seeing beggars approach.
Even when giving out of necessity, one feels as though one’s own flesh were being cut away, giving rise to deep pain and regret.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable sentient beings who, driven by stinginess and greed, amass wealth and property yet do not even enjoy it themselves, let alone share it with their parents, wives, children, servants, laborers, or those who come to beg.
When those sentient beings pass away from there, they are reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts or among the animals.

Because they once briefly heard the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha during their time as humans, they now, while in the miserable realms, briefly remember the name of that Tathāgata. At the very moment of such recollection, they pass away from those places and are reborn among human beings. They obtain the memory of their past lives, fear the suffering of the miserable realms, take no pleasure in sensual desires, delight in practicing generosity, praise those who give, and have no greed or stinginess regarding anything they possess.
"If he can gradually bestow even his head, eyes, hands, feet, flesh, blood, and limbs upon those who come to beg for them, how much more so other material wealth.
The commentary states:
"This is the second [section], the accomplishment of the merit of hearing the name in foreign lands."

Within this, there are five [sections], because they cause those who hear them to eliminate the five kinds of obstacles to giving, ethical discipline, and the cultivation of the ten paths of wholesome action that lead to rebirth in blissful realms.
Now, this first section clarifies the elimination of obstacles to meritorious actions consisting of giving.
This consists of three sections:
first, the section revealing the nature of the hindrances, as stated in the sutra: "Not recognizing good and evil, even when a beggar comes to ask.
Here, "not recognizing evil" refers solely to greed and stinginess.
Those who do not recognize what is wholesome do so because they do not understand the nature of giving;
they fail to distinguish between good and evil.

Because they are deluded and devoid of wisdom, harboring only greed and stinginess, and because they lack the faculty of faith and thus do not understand giving and other virtues, they amass much wealth and refuse to relinquish it.
The second is the section showing the faults and afflictions of the obstacles, as the sūtra states: "Those sentient beings are born among ghosts and animals.
Because of stinginess and greed they are born in the realm of hungry ghosts; because of delusion they are born in the animal destiny.
Third is hearing the gateway of the Buddha’s supreme benefits, as stated in the sutra: "From his former existence as a human being...
how much more so with other material wealth. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If there are sentient beings who, although they have received the various precepts from the Tathāgata, violate the śīla;
or those who, although they do not violate the śīla, violate the rules of conduct (ācāra);
or those who, although they do not corrupt their śīla or rules of conduct, nevertheless destroy right view (samyagdṛṣṭi).
There are those who, while not destroying right view, abandon extensive learning;
they are unable to comprehend the profound meaning of the sūtras spoken by the Buddha.

There are others who, despite being extensively learned, harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*); because their minds are shrouded by this overweening pride, they judge themselves as correct and others as wrong, disparaging and slandering the true Dharma, and thus become partisans of Māra.
Thus, these foolish people, having practiced wrong views themselves, cause immeasurable koṭis of sentient beings to fall into great perilous pits.
These sentient beings will wander endlessly through the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
If one hears the name of this Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, one will abandon unwholesome conduct, cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and not fall into the evil destinies.

Should there be those who are unable to abandon unwholesome conduct and practice wholesome dharmas, and thus fall into the evil destinies, by the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow, they shall temporarily hear his name in their presence; at the end of their lives there, they shall return to the human realm, attain right view, diligence, and well-disciplined intentions, and be able to leave the household life for the homeless state. Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, they will receive and uphold the precepts without violation, possess right view and great learning, understand profound meanings, be free from overweening pride, and not slander the true Dharma. They shall not become companions of Māra, but will gradually cultivate the various practices of a bodhisattva and swiftly attain perfection.
The commentary states:
This reveals that which can eliminate the obstacle to the merit of the nature of precepts.
This also consists of three gates, as should be understood from what preceded.
The first gate has three parts:
first, the obstacle to the precept of restraining conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), as the sūtra says, "to violate the rules of *śīla*.
Here, *śīla* refers to the prātimokṣa precepts.
Regarding "rules of conduct," this refers to dwelling in right awareness during coming and going and other such activities.
Second is the obstacle to the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas, as the sutra states: "destroying right view, abandoning extensive learning, and increasing conceit."
The third is the obstacle to the precept of gathering sentient beings, as the sūtra states: "Furthermore, it causes immeasurable koṭis of sentient beings to fall into great precipitous pits.
Next, regarding the gate that demonstrates the faults and afflictions of these obstacles, it is as the sūtra states: "They transmigrate through the hells and other realms without end."
Regarding "later hearing of the Buddha’s gate of supreme victory," it is as the sutra says: "until the three aggregates are swiftly fulfilled. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If sentient beings are stingy, greedy, jealous, and envious, praising themselves and disparaging others, they shall fall into the three evil destinies and undergo various intense sufferings for immeasurable thousands of years.

Having undergone such intense suffering, their lives there come to an end and they are reborn in the human realm. They become oxen, horses, camels, donkeys, or mules, constantly tormented by whips and lashes, oppressed by hunger and thirst, and always forced to carry heavy burdens along the roads.
Or, if they obtain a human birth, they are born into lowly circumstances as servants or slaves, subjected to the commands of others and never possessing any autonomy.

If, in a former life among humans, one had heard the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, by virtue of this wholesome cause, one now recalls it again and takes refuge with a sincere heart; through the Buddha’s spiritual power, one shall be liberated from all sufferings, possess keen faculties, and be endowed with wisdom and extensive learning. Constantly seeking the supreme Dharma and always meeting virtuous friends, one shall forever sever the snares of Māra, shatter the husks of ignorance, and dry up the river of afflictions, thereby attaining liberation from all birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
The commentary states:
This reveals that which can eliminate the obstacles to meritorious action consisting of cultivation.
It likewise has three gates:
First is the gate revealing the intrinsic nature of the obstacles, as stated in the Sūtra: "Miserliness, greed, envy, jealousy, self-praise, and disparaging others.
Among these, miserliness and greed can obstruct the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because they prevent the giving of happiness.
Envy obstructs sympathetic joy because one does not rejoice in the merit of others.
Slander and praise obstruct compassion because they cause affliction and harm.
The first three [afflictions] obstruct the nature of equanimity because they are defiled.
Because the sequence of the discourse is thus established, there is no contradiction.
Second, regarding the gate that demonstrates the faults and afflictions of obstacles, it is as the sutra states: "falling into the three evil destinies and undergoing suffering."
Third, regarding the gateway of hearing the supreme benefits of the Buddha, it is as stated in the sutra: "up to and including the eternal destruction of the four kinds of Māras.
This may be understood according to the text. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are sentient beings who delight in discord, engaging in mutual strife, litigation, and turmoil that distresses both themselves and others; who, through body, speech, and mind, create and increase various types of evil karma; who constantly engage in harmful acts against one another and plot to injure each other; who summon deities of mountains, forests, trees, and burial mounds; who kill living beings and take their flesh and blood to offer as sacrifices to yakṣas, rākṣasas, and the like; who write down the names of their enemies, fashion their images, and curse them with malevolent incantations; and who employ sorcery, spirit-possession, and the raising of corpse-ghosts to cut off the lives of others and destroy their bodies.

If these sentient beings should hear the name of this Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, none of those evil matters will be able to harm them. All will develop mutual thoughts of loving-kindness, seeking their benefit and peace; they will be free from intent to injure or afflict, as well as resentment, and each will rejoice, finding contentment in what they receive for themselves, refraining from mutual aggression while instead providing mutual assistance.
The commentary states:
This reveals that which can eliminate the obstacles to the ten paths of wholesome action.
There are also three gates:
First, regarding the obstruction to its intrinsic nature: as the sūtra states, "delighting in separation... up to increasing various evil karmas.
Delighting in separation means that the three karmic paths of the mind are all capable of causing others to be separated from what they desire.
They further engage in mutual strife and litigation, their speech being inconsistent with the principles of the four karmas, thereby frequently inciting disputes.

They afflict and disturb both themselves and others: through the three paths of bodily karma, if the results of these three types of action are brought to fruition, they disturb others; if the results are not brought to fruition, they disturb themselves.

Regarding the fault of the two hindrances: it refers to how one's own evil invites harm from others, as the Sūtra states: "They constantly engage in harmful acts against one another, even going so far as to raise corpse-demons through incantations to sever and destroy one's life-force."
Regarding the three doors of benefit: if they are already free from harm in the present, how much more so will they be from future suffering?
This is clear from the text. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are members of the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—as well as other sons and daughters of good family with pure faith—who are able to observe the eightfold precepts for one year, or who observe the training rules for three months, and who, by means of these roots of virtue, vow to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss in the presence of the Buddha Amitāyus to hear the True Dharma, yet have not yet attained certainty: if they hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, then at the time of their death, eight bodhisattvas will arrive by means of supernatural powers to show them the way, and they shall be spontaneously reborn within various multicolored flowers made of many jewels in that realm.

Some may, because of this, be born in the heavens; though born among the gods, their original roots of goodness are not yet exhausted, and they will not again be reborn in other evil realms. When their lifespan in heaven ends, they return to the human world, perhaps becoming a Wheel-Turning King who governs the four continents with sovereign majesty, establishing countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in the ten paths of wholesome action;

or they may be born into great families of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or householders, possessing abundant wealth and overflowing treasuries, with handsome features and a full circle of kin, being intelligent and wise, and as brave, robust, and majestic as mighty warriors.
If it is a woman who hears the name of the World-Honored One, Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata, and receives and upholds it with a sincere heart, she shall never again receive a female body hereafter.
The commentary states:
This demonstrates that [the practice] can eliminate the obstacles to rebirth in a happy realm.
This further has two parts:
first, manifesting the removal of obstacles to the arising of joy in the pure land, as the sutra says, "born in the world of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the practice of upholding the eightfold precepts for months or years, Master Mai said:
"Regarding 'one year,' it means that within one year there are six days each month; that is, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of both the dark and light fortnights."

Regarding "or three months": if one cannot observe the six fast days each month throughout the year, but can maintain the three long months—namely, the first, fifth, and ninth months—observing the fast during the first month of each of these three periods of exclusion, this signifies that one constantly cultivates goodness throughout the year.
As the Song edition states: "One should constantly observe the six monthly fasts and the three annual long fasts.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 13, says: "On the days of fasting, those who uphold the eight precepts [protect themselves from] evil spirits who pursue people on such days, desiring to snatch away their lives."
At the beginning of the kalpa, the sages taught people to observe the fast; however, they did not receive the eight precepts, but simply took one day of not eating as the fast.
Later, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he established the eight precepts.
Question: Between the five precepts and the eight precepts, which is superior? Answer:
Due to specific causes and conditions, the two precepts are equal, as they differ respectively in terms of time and constituent parts.
Question:
If even ten recitations of the name can lead to rebirth there, why would one year not suffice?
Answer: Because there is a distinction between being courageous and being complacent.
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom) says: "A mind that is fierce at the moment of death surpasses a hundred years of merit."
Regarding "spontaneous birth" (upapāduka): for example, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the woman from the mango tree was born from the flowers of that tree and is thus called moisture-born;
since [beings in] the Pure Land are born from flowers, why are they called spontaneously born?
Master Mai said:
“Before entrusting one’s life to birth, the tree possesses moisture.
In the Pure Land, the lotus flowers bring about transformational birth for humans.”

The second [type of obstacle] is the hindrance to removing impurities from the land and taking birth in a happy realm, as stated in the sūtra: "Or some, because of this, are born in the heavens," and so forth.
This further comprises four types: birth in the heavens, as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), in a noble and eminent family, and as a male body; these may be understood according to the text.
The Upper Part of the *Benyuan Yaoshi Jing Guji* (Ancient Traces of the Sutra on the Original Vows of the Medicine Master) concludes here.
[This is followed by] the Lower Part of the *Benyuan Yaoshi Jing Guji*,
titled the *Yaoshi Liuliguang Rulai Benyuan Gongde Jing* (Sutra on the Merit of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light).
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One!

I vow that during the period of the Semblance Dharma, by means of various skillful expedients, I shall cause all faithful sons and daughters of good family to hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha; even while they are asleep, I shall awaken their ears to the name of the Buddha."

"Bhagavān! If one receives, maintains, recites, or reads this sutra, or further explains and reveals it for others; or if one writes it oneself or instructs others to write it; and if one reveres and honors it with various flowers, incense, unguents, burning incense, flower garlands, necklaces, banners, canopies, and music; and if one makes a pouch from five-colored silks to contain it, sweeps and sprinkles a clean place, prepares a high seat, and places it therein—at that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of other celestial hosts, will all go to that place to make offerings and provide protection."
“World-Honored One!

Wherever this jewel of a sutra circulates, if there are those who can receive and uphold it—by virtue of the original vows and merits of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, and through hearing his name—it should be known that in such places there shall be no more untimely deaths; nor shall they have their vital energy stolen by various evil spirits and ghosts. Even if it has already been stolen, it shall be restored as before, and their body and mind will be peaceful and happy.”
The commentary states:
This is the second major section, the Gate of Exhorting Sentient Beings to Benefit Others.
It consists of five sub-sections:

First is the gate of awakening through the power of vows, as the sutra states: "I vow that during the period of the Semblance Dharma, I shall employ skillful means to cause [beings] to hear the name of the Tathāgata; by virtue of upholding, reciting, and making offerings to this sutra, the assembly of devas shall protect them so that no calamities or misfortunes occur."
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"So it is, so it is, just as you have said. Mañjuśrī!"

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who wish to make offerings to that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, they should first fashion an image of that Buddha, arrange a pure seat, and install it therein; they should scatter various flowers, burn various incenses, and adorn the place with various banners and streamers.
For seven days and seven nights, one should observe the eightfold precepts, consume pure food, bathe until fragrant and clean, and wear new, pure garments.

One should give rise to a mind free from defilement and turbidity, a mind free from anger and malice, and toward all sentient beings, cultivate a mind of equanimity characterized by altruism, peace, compassion, joy, and relinquishment; then, with the beating of drums and the singing of praises, one should circumambulate the Buddha image to the right.

Furthermore, one should recollect the merit of that Tathāgata’s original vows, read and recite this sutra, contemplate its meaning, and explain and reveal it to others; then all their aspirations and wishes will be fulfilled: those who seek long life shall obtain long life, those who seek wealth and abundance shall obtain wealth and abundance, those who seek official rank shall obtain official rank, and those who seek sons or daughters shall obtain sons or daughters.
Furthermore, if there is a person who suddenly experiences a bad dream, sees various evil omens, or if strange birds gather or a hundred anomalies appear at their dwelling place—

if such a person reverently makes offerings with various exquisite requisites to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, then all those bad dreams, evil omens, and inauspicious signs will entirely vanish and be unable to cause harm.

Should there be fears of water, fire, knives, or poison; of precipices; or of evil elephants, lions, tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears; or of venomous snakes, malicious scorpions, centipedes, millipedes, mosquitoes, and gadflies—if one can with a sincere heart recollect that Buddha, paying him reverence and making offerings, one shall be liberated from all such terrors.
If other countries are invaded and disturbed, or if thieves and rebels cause turmoil, those who mindfully recollect and pay homage to that Tathāgata shall likewise all be liberated.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who, for as long as they live, do not serve other deities but instead single-mindedly take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts—whether the five precepts, the ten precepts, the four hundred bodhisattva precepts, the two hundred and fifty bhikṣu precepts, or the five hundred bhikṣuṇī precepts.
Among those who have received the precepts, there may be some who commit transgressions and fear falling into the evil realms;
yet if they can single-mindedly recite the name of that Buddha and reverently make offerings to him, they will certainly not undergo rebirth in the three evil realms.

If there are women who, when facing the time of childbirth, undergo extreme suffering, should they with a sincere heart invoke the name, pay homage, praise, and reverently make offerings to that Tathāgata, all their sufferings will be eliminated. The child they give birth to will have complete physical faculties and a handsome appearance, bringing joy to those who see him; he will possess sharp and intelligent faculties, be secure and free from illness, and no non-human beings shall steal away his vital energy.
The commentary states:
This is the second section, the Gate of the Tathāgata’s Confirmation.
Within it, there are two parts:
First, making offerings is clarified; second, the benefits obtained are explained.
There are three kinds of offerings:
first, material offerings, as the sutra states: "Constructing images and even adorning their locations."
Second is the offering of correct practice, as the sutra states: "observing the precepts for seven days up to the mind of equanimity.
Third is the offering of the three karmas, as the sutra states: "playing drums and music, singing praises, up to expounding and elucidating [the Dharma]."
There are three kinds of benefits:
first, the gate of fulfilling what is sought, as the sūtra says, "according to their wishes and desires, up to obtaining sons and daughters";
second, the gate of eliminating what is loathed, as the sūtra says, "if there are further people, up to all being liberated."
The third is the gate of destroying precepts and departing from suffering; herein there are two parts.

First is the destruction of precepts in the present body out of fear of future suffering, as the sūtra says: "Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, [he] will not undergo birth in the three evil realms," and so forth.

Regarding the four hundred precepts for bodhisattvas herein, they differ in their expansion and contraction because the Tathāgata taught extensively or concisely according to what was appropriate for his listeners.

For instance, the Vaipulya sūtras speak of four grave offenses and twenty-eight light offenses; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of four grave offenses and forty-five light offenses; and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* speaks of ten grave offenses and forty-eight light offenses—thus there are differences among them.

However, while this single manuscript reads "twenty-four precepts" in the Song translation and "one hundred four precepts" in the Sui translation, this is because there are discrepancies among the various Sanskrit manuscripts.
Second, because in a previous life they violated the precepts and consequently underwent the suffering of female childbirth.
As the Sūtra says: "There may be women who even rob them of their vital essence.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
Just as I have extolled all the merits of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaisajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, this is the profound sphere of practice of all Buddhas, which is difficult to comprehend.
"Do you believe this? Ānanda replied,
"Venerable World-Honored One!"
I harbor no doubt or uncertainty regarding the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because the bodily, vocal, and mental actions of all Tathāgatas are entirely pure.
World-Honored One!
These orbs of the sun and moon might be made to fall, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, might be caused to tremble; yet there is no difference in what the Buddhas have spoken.
"Bhagavān! There are sentient beings who lack the faculty of faith; when they hear it said that the Buddhas have such profound spheres of activity, they think to themselves:
'How is it that by merely recollecting the name of a single Buddha, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, one obtains such vast merit and benefits?'"
Due to this lack of faith, they instead give rise to slander.
Throughout the long night, they lose great benefit and happiness, falling into the various evil realms where they will transmigrate without end.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

If these sentient beings hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, and with a sincere heart uphold it without giving rise to doubt or hesitation, it is impossible for them to fall into the evil realms.
Ānanda! This is the profound sphere of activity of all Buddhas, difficult to believe and understand.
That you are now able to receive it, you should know that this is entirely through the majestic power of the Tathāgata.

Ānanda! All śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended to the stages are entirely unable to believe and understand it as it truly is, with the sole exception of bodhisattvas bound to only one more birth (ekajātipratibaddha).

Ānanda! Human birth is difficult to obtain; to have faith, reverence, and respect for the Triple Gem is likewise difficult to obtain; and to hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, is even more difficult than that.

Ānanda! Regarding that Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha, his immeasurable bodhisattva practices, his immeasurable skillful means, and his immeasurable vast and great vows—if I were to explain them at length for an eon or even more than an eon, the eon might quickly come to an end, yet the Buddha’s practices, vows, and skillful means would never be exhausted.
The commentary states:
This is the third section, the gate of the benefits and harms of destroying faith.
It consists of four sub-sections:
First is the gate of the certainty of the Buddha’s words, as the sūtra states: "As I have extolled them, so it is; there is no difference between what I say and what all Buddhas say.
Second is the gate of the decline resulting from slander, as the sūtra states: "There are sentient beings who [slander], and thus they wander through saṃsāra without end."
Third is the section on the benefits obtained through reverent faith, as the sutra states: "The Buddha told Ānanda... it is impossible for them to fall into the evil destinies.
Fourth is the section on exhorting others to believe and accept [the teaching], as the sutra states: "Ānanda... there shall be no end to it."

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva-mahāsattva named Jue-tuo (Trāṇamukta). He rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous World-Honored One!"

During the period when the Semblance Dharma prevails, there will be sentient beings oppressed by various afflictions; long-term illness will cause them to become emaciated and unable to eat or drink; their throats and lips will become parched, they will see all directions as dark, and the signs of death will appear before them.
Although his parents, relatives, friends, and acquaintances weep and surround him, he himself lies where he is, seeing the messengers of Yama leading his consciousness before the Dharma King Yama.
However, all sentient beings possess an innate deity who records every action they perform, whether sinful or meritorious, and delivers this complete record to King Yama, the Lord of Dharma.
At that time, the king shall interrogate the person regarding their deeds and calculate their merits and transgressions, then pass judgment accordingly.

If the patient’s relatives and friends can take refuge in the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, invite the assembly of monks to recite this sutra, light seven-tiered lamps, and hang five-colored banners for the prolongation of life, there may be a place where the patient's consciousness returns; as if in a dream, they will clearly see themselves.

Whether after seven days, twenty-one days, thirty-five days, or forty-nine days, when that consciousness returns, it is like awakening from a dream; one will clearly remember and know the retributive fruits obtained from one's wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Because they have personally witnessed the retribution of karmic results, they will not commit any evil deeds even at the cost of their lives.

Therefore, sons and daughters of noble family who possess pure faith should all uphold the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha and, according to their capacity, reverently make offerings to him.
The commentary states:
This is the fourth section, the Gate of Providing Assistance for Image-Making.
It consists of two sub-sections:
First, the gate of assisting what is to be done; second, the gate of assisting for the sake of victory.
Regarding the first, as for "what is to be done," it is as stated in the sutra: "During the period of the Semblance Dharma, and so forth, until they are eradicated."
As for Yama, in the Tang language it means "Tranquil Rest," because he awakens sinners to cease all evil.
Precisely for this reason, although he is categorized within the realm of ghosts, he is also called the Dharma King.
This means that by the power of karma, four objective aspects manifest to the consciousness of the dying patient:
first, the messengers of Yama; second, one's own departed consciousness; third, King Yama; and fourth, the co-emergent deity.
It is traditionally said that because the fundamental consciousness and the body arise together, they are termed "co-emergent.

Because the spirit is capable of perfuming [the seeds], it is said to possess the capacity for writing and upholding [the teachings] as a manifestation of the Dharma King; therefore, it is said to "bestow" [them].
Through the power of karma, manifestations resembling divine forms appear.
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Those born together and sharing the same name are all produced from a single divinity."
Regarding the second, the gateway of the benefits of supportive conditions: as stated in the Sūtra, "At that time, that sick person... even his various evil karmas...
Herein, there are five types of supporting requisites: taking refuge in the Buddha, requesting the Saṃgha, turning the wheel of Dharma, lighting lamps, and hoisting banners.
A lamp signifies illumination; a banner signifies leading.
Because one must rescue those submerged in darkness, banners and lamps are required.
As for the seven tiers and five colors, there is no specific explanation for their purpose.
If one infers this by means of its underlying principle, it is because the sevenfold offenses are suppressed and the five directions are harmonized.
As for the statement that "there may be a place where that consciousness returns," the term "may" is used to distinguish this from fixed karma (niyata-karma).
Regarding the statement that it may last for seven days up to forty-nine days, this is intended because the life-span in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) lasts for seven days.
However, the subsequent periods of three intervals of two weeks each are taught to clarify that, according to the actual fact, [the deceased] has not yet departed from the body.
The transmitters all say that, in reality, the conscious spirit has never left the body.
At that time, Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Rescuer from Distress:
"O son of good family!"
"How should one reverently make offerings to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha?
Furthermore, how should the life-prolonging banners and lamps be constructed?
Bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla replied:
"Virtuous One!

If there is a sick person who wishes to be freed from the suffering of illness, one should, for that person's sake, observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) for seven days and seven nights. One should provide offerings of food, drink, and other necessary requisites to the community of bhikṣus according to one's means; one should worship and make offerings to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha, during the six periods of day and night; one should recite this sūtra forty-nine times and light forty-nine lamps."
One should fashion seven images of that Tathāgata, and before each image place seven lamps; each lamp should be as large as a chariot wheel, and their light must not cease for forty-nine days.
One should fashion five-colored silk banners forty-nine spans long.
One should also release various kinds of sentient beings up to forty-nine in number; thus one may transcend the perils of danger and distress, and shall not be seized by various malevolent ghosts.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

When calamities arise for kṣatriya kings who have received the consecration—namely, the calamity of epidemics among the populace, the calamity of invasion by foreign nations, the calamity of rebellion within one's own realm, the calamity of portents in the stars and constellations, the calamity of eclipses of the sun and moon, the calamity of unseasonable winds and rain, and the calamity of drought when the time has passed.

At that time, those Kṣatriya consecrated kings and others should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings, release all those who are imprisoned, and perform the aforementioned methods of offering to worship that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabha.

By virtue of these roots of goodness and the power of that Tathāgata’s original vow, his realm shall immediately attain peace and stability; wind and rain will fall in their proper seasons, and crops will ripen. All sentient beings will be free from illness and live in joy. Within that land, there shall be no violent yakṣas or other spirits who afflict sentient beings, and all evil omens shall vanish. Furthermore, the life span, physical strength, health, and sovereignty of the consecrated kṣatriya kings and others shall all be increased.

Ānanda! If the Emperor, the Empress, the Crown Prince, ministers and high officials, ladies of the inner court, or the various officials and commoners suffer from illness or other calamities, they should likewise erect five-colored divine banners, light lamps to maintain illumination, release living beings, scatter flowers of various colors, and burn many kinds of famous incense; thus their illnesses will be cured and they will be liberated from all hardships.
The commentary states:
From here below is the fifth section, the Gate of Question and Answer for Resolving Difficulties.
This contains two parts:
First, because it consists of a question and answer; second, because it resolves difficulties.
This is the first [section].
Within the answer, there are two parts:
First, the answer is difficult to provide because it is based on specific illnesses, as extensively explained in the sutra where the Bodhisattva Trāṇamukta says, "and so forth.
What is taught here pertains to the ultimate limit; even if not fully complete, there is still benefit, as the preceding sutra states, "one should make offerings according to one's capacity."
The *Dharmasamāja-sūtra* states: "Even one lamp may suffice for the poor.
Regarding the placement of seven lamps at each [altar], Master Mai said:
"Before each image, construct seven wheel-shaped lamps, shaped like chariot wheels."
"Before each statue and its pedestal, place one wheel-lamp; upon each wheel, install seven lamps.
This was the subsequent response regarding national calamities.
This, in turn, has two parts:
This is because of the difficulty of national boundaries and the difficulty of kinsmen, as stated in the Sūtra: "Furthermore, Ānanda, [it protects] up to liberation from all difficulties.
The meaning here is that it not only rescues the sick person but also delivers one from the perils of kings.
A kingdom has seven calamities, which can be understood according to the text.

As for the consecrated king (*abhiṣeka-rāja*), he is the supreme sovereign of the greatest nation; at the time of his enthronement, the various minor kings and all the ministers each take water from the four great oceans and pour it over his head.
The phrase "the realm is peaceful and secure" refers to the removal of the second and third calamities.
"Wind and rain are timely and the harvests are bountiful" refers to the removal of the sixth and seventh calamities.
"Freedom from disease and malevolent spirits" refers to the removal of the first calamity.
Regarding the disappearance of evil signs: this is because the fourth and fifth difficulties are difficult to eliminate.
The difficulty concerning the king’s retinue may be understood according to the text.
At that time, Ānanda asked the Bodhisattva Jue tuo (Tārāvatī):
"Good son! How can a life that has already been exhausted be increased?
The Bodhisattva Rescuer and Deliverer replied:
"Virtuous One!
Have you not heard the Tathāgata say that there are nine forms of untimely death?
For this reason, I urge you to create life-prolonging banners and lamps, and to cultivate various meritorious virtues."
Because they have cultivated merit, throughout their entire lifespans they do not undergo suffering or affliction.
Ānanda asked: "What are the nine untimely deaths?"
The Bodhisattva Jiu-tuo said:

"There are sentient beings whose illnesses, though light, have neither medicine nor a caregiver; furthermore, even if they encounter a physician who prescribes the wrong medicine, they die prematurely when they ought not to have died."

Furthermore, they believe the worldly teachers of demons, heterodox paths, and sorcerers who falsely proclaim calamities and blessings; thus, they become terrified and agitated, their minds failing to remain upright. They consult diviners to seek out misfortune, slaughter various kinds of sentient beings to offer as sacrifices to the spirits, summon various ghosts and spirits, and pray for blessings and protection, hoping thereby to extend their years, yet in the end they cannot achieve this.
Being foolish and deluded, they believe in heterodox and inverted views, which ultimately causes them to die an untimely death and enter hell from which there is no period of escape.
This is called the first untimely death.
Second, they are executed by the laws of the king.
Third, those who indulge in hunting and games, are addicted to lust and wine, and are dissolute and unrestrained, will have their vital essence forcibly snatched away by non-human beings.
Fourth, they will be suddenly consumed by fire.
Fifth, they are unexpectedly drowned by water.
Sixth, they are unexpectedly devoured by various kinds of vicious beasts.
Seventh, they are unexpectedly fall from mountain precipices.
Eighth, they will be suddenly struck down and harmed by poisons, malevolent incantations, curses, or reanimated corpses.
Ninth, they will be overcome by hunger and thirst, unable to obtain food or drink, and thus meet an untimely death.
This is what the Tathāgata has briefly described as the nine kinds of untimely death.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable other forms of untimely death that are difficult to describe in detail. Moreover, Ānanda:

That King Yama, Lord of Death, presides over the records of the world’s registers; if sentient beings are unfilial, commit the five heinous crimes, bring disgrace upon the Triple Gem, subvert the laws between ruler and subject, or destroy their faith and precepts, King Yama, the Dharma King, shall examine and punish them according to the gravity of their offenses.

For this reason, I now exhort all sentient beings to light lamps, create banners, release living beings, and cultivate merit, so that they may cross over suffering and distress and not encounter various calamities.
Commentary: This constitutes the section on resolving difficulties.
Within this, there are five parts:
first, the objection; second, the resolution; third, the inquiry; fourth, the explanation; and fifth, the conclusion.

Regarding the resolution: the nine types of untimely death are all indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*), because they are the outflowing results (*niṣyanda-phala*) that correspond to past karma, and because if one has supportive merit, their duration can be extended.

Regarding the statement that one cannot achieve [the goal] by such means: killing shortens one's life and eating meat brings much illness; yet how could one extend one’s own lifespan by ending the lives of others?
Even if the resulting illness is slight, it destroys the karma of longevity and leads to untimely death and entry into hell—this is the intended meaning here.
Regarding the "binding of the intention": if one’s life is not extended, it falls under the jurisdiction of Yama; thus the textual meaning is clear.

At that time, there were twelve yakṣa generals present among the assembly, seated together. They were: the general Piṅgala, the general Vajrapāṇi, the general Mecaka, the general Andhara, the general Acala, the general Saṃdhara, the general Indrāla, the general Pīvara, the general Mahāla, the general Candāla, the general Caturaka, and the general Vikarāla. Each of these twelve yakṣa generals had seven thousand yakṣas as their retinue. Simultaneously raising their voices, they addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!”

Having now received the Buddha’s majestic power, we have been able to hear the name of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha; henceforth, we shall no longer have any fear of the miserable realms.

We shall lead one another with a single mind, and for as long as we live, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; we vow to bear the burden of all sentient beings, acting for their benefit, welfare, and peace and happiness.

In whatever village, city, town, or forest retreat this sutra may be circulated, or wherever there are those who uphold the name of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha and reverently make offerings to him, we and our retinues shall protect such persons, causing them all to be liberated from every suffering and hardship, and ensuring that all their aspirations and requests are fully satisfied.

If there are those who suffer from illness or calamity and seek liberation, they should likewise recite this sutra; they should tie my name with thread of five colors, and once their wishes are fulfilled, they should then untie the knots.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the great yakṣa generals, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Great yakṣa generals!"

If you wish to repay the kindness and virtue of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha, you should always act in this way to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
Below this is the fifth section, the accomplishment of repaying kindness through the benefits obtained by the yakṣa general.
This section contains three parts:
First, the sūtra compiler lists the names; next, the yakṣas make their vow; finally, the Tathāgata grants his approval—the structure of the text is thus clear.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should this Dharma-gate be called?
How should we uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

This Dharma gate is called "The Exposition of the Merit of the Original Vows of the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha"; it is also called "The Exposition of the Beneficial Incantations for Sentient Beings and the Vows of the Twelve Divine Generals"; and it is also called "The Eradication of All Karmic Obstructions. It should be upheld in this manner.

When the Bhagavān had spoken these words, all the great bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas and the great śrāvakas, as well as the kings, ministers, brahmins, householders, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had taught, were filled with great joy; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The commentary states:
From here below is the third section, the "Practice of Joy upon Hearing the Name.
The phrase "it should be upheld in this manner" answers the second question.
One should accept and uphold [the teaching] in accordance with the phenomena signified by these three names.
